Every cell you've met so far has a nucleus, a membrane and cytoplasm, but a leaf cell has a few extra parts that a cheek cell doesn't, and each one is there for a reason.

## Engage: what's missing?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students often think animal cells have walls, or that plants don't need mitochondria because they make their own food; the options test both."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Which of these does a plant leaf cell have that a cheek cell does not?"
  options: ["A cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole", "Mitochondria", "A nucleus", "A cell membrane"]
  actual: "A cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Both cells have mitochondria, a nucleus and a membrane: plants release energy from food just as animals do."
```

## Explore: compare the cells

```step
stage: run
insight: "Finding the plant-only parts side by side with an animal cell, then the mitochondria in both, separates 'plant-specific' from 'every cell'."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#compare", height: 600 }
tasks:
  - starter: "boards.yml#compare"
    check: { type: board, text: "Find the three parts that only the plant cell has.", when: "n = k" }
    hint: ["What can you see in the leaf cell that the cheek cell doesn't have at all?", "Thin outlines count as parts too, so click right on the lines around the leaf cell and read the name under the board."]
  - starter: "boards.yml#mito"
    check: { type: board, text: "Now find the mitochondria in both cells.", when: "n = k" }
    hint: ["Mitochondria release energy, and both cells need energy, so look for the same small shapes in each one.", "They're the small orange capsules, and the line under the board tells you how many you've still got to find."]
```

### In both

## Explain: what each part is for

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Tying each plant-only part to something plants need and animals don't (support without a skeleton, making food, staying firm) explains the differences instead of listing them."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each part to its job."
      pairs:
        - ["Cell wall", "Rigid support, so the plant holds its shape without a skeleton"]
        - ["Chloroplast", "Photosynthesis: captures light to make glucose"]
        - ["Large vacuole", "Holds cell sap and keeps the cell firm"]
        - ["Mitochondria", "Release energy from food (respiration)"]
        - ["Ribosomes", "Make proteins"]
      explain: "The first three are only in plant cells (walls also in fungi and bacteria). Mitochondria and ribosomes are in both."
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Plant cells only, or both plant and animal cells?"
      options: ["Plant only", "Both"]
      items:
        - ["Cell wall", "Plant only"]
        - ["Chloroplasts", "Plant only"]
        - ["Large permanent vacuole", "Plant only"]
        - ["Mitochondria", "Both", "Plants respire too, day and night."]
        - ["Ribosomes", "Both"]
        - ["Nucleus", "Both"]
    hint: ["Once a plant has made its glucose, how does it get the energy back out of it to use?", "Think back to the board you just used: which cells did you find the mitochondria in?"]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why don't animal cells need chloroplasts?"
      options: ["Animals get their food by eating, so they don't make it from light", "Animals live where there is no light", "Animal cells are too small for chloroplasts"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Most animals live in light; it is how they get food that differs.", "Size is not the reason."]
      explain: "Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; animals eat. Each cell's parts match how the organism lives."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A lettuce leaf goes limp when it loses water. Which part explains this?"
      options: ["The vacuoles shrink, so the cells push less against their walls", "The chloroplasts stop working", "The cell walls dissolve"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Chloroplasts make food; they don't hold the leaf up.", "Walls stay; it's the pressure inside that drops."]
      explain: "A full vacuole presses the cell against its wall and keeps it firm. Lose water and the cell goes soft: the leaf wilts. Put it in water and it firms up again."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A muscle cell has far more mitochondria than a skin cell. Why?"
      options: ["Contracting needs a lot of energy, and mitochondria release it", "Muscle cells are bigger", "Mitochondria make muscles strong"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Size alone doesn't explain it; the job does.", "They supply energy; the protein fibres do the pulling."]
      explain: "Cells have the parts their job needs, in the numbers it needs: same DNA, different organelles."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name the parts only plant cells have and explain what each is for, and say which parts all these cells share." }
```

## Elaborate: a root hair cell

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "A plant cell without chloroplasts shows that parts depend on the cell's job, not just on being a plant."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#roothair", height: 600 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Find every part of the root hair cell and the leaf cell.", when: "n = k" }
    hint: "Thin parts like the wall and the membrane are easy to miss, so if the count under the board isn't full, click right along the outlines of both cells."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Root hair cells have no chloroplasts. Why not?"
      options: ["They are underground, with no light to photosynthesise; their job is taking in water", "They are not plant cells", "Chloroplasts would make them too heavy"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "They are plant cells: they have walls and vacuoles.", "Weight is not the reason."]
      explain: "A cell has the parts its job needs. Chloroplasts in the dark would be useless."
    hint: "Do roots get any light down in the soil? And what do chloroplasts need light for?"
```

      feedback: [null, "Animal gland cells have no chloroplasts.", "Large vacuoles are a plant cell feature."]

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about plant and animal cells with the cells on the board." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- Only plant cells have a **cell wall** (support), **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis) and a **large vacuole** (keeps the cell firm, stores sap).
- Plant and animal cells both have a nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, **mitochondria** (release energy from food) and **ribosomes** (make proteins).
- How many of each part a cell has depends on its job: muscle cells have many mitochondria; root hair cells have no chloroplasts.

```teacher
summary: Students identify the cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole as
  plant-only structures and explain each, describe mitochondria and ribosomes in
  both cell types, and link a cell's organelles to its job (AC9S8U01, nodes 4
  and 5).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 7 min · Explain 11 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical
  adds 3 min, Wider about 3 min
goals:
  - I can name the parts only plant cells have and say what each is for.
  - I can say which parts plant and animal cells share.
  - I can explain why some cells have more of one part than others.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it pairs with onion
  and cheek cell slides. Set the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical`
  (default) or `wider`. One lesson for two nodes (plant-specific structures,
  other organelles), after What does every cell have? and before Why are cells
  different shapes?


  Not hinge nodes. The misconceptions: animal cells have walls; plants don't
  need mitochondria because they photosynthesise; every plant cell has
  chloroplasts. The prediction and the Typical step target them.


  Board notes: the diagrams are not to scale and show only some mitochondria and
  chloroplasts. Ribosomes are too small to draw at this scale, so they appear in
  the questions only.
running:
  - "Engage: tally the predictions. 'Mitochondria' means the student thinks
    plants don't respire."
  - "Explore: ask what the plant needs that each plant-only part provides."
  - "Explain: the matching and the sort are the success criteria; the lettuce
    and muscle questions are the 'why'."
  - "In your own words: the labelled pair of cells is the evidence."
struggle: Explaining why a part exists, not just naming it. When a student lists
  parts, ask what the plant would do without that part, and wait for the reason
  before moving on.
stuck:
  - see: A student gives an animal cell a cell wall.
    ask: What holds an animal up?
    fix: A skeleton (or water pressure in soft animals). Animal cells have a
      flexible membrane only.
  - see: A student says plants don't have mitochondria because they make their own
      food.
    ask: Once a plant has made glucose, how does it get energy out of it?
    fix: Respiration, in mitochondria, like animals. Plants respire all the time,
      day and night.
  - see: A student thinks every plant cell is green.
    ask: Do roots get light?
    fix: No, so root cells have no chloroplasts. Parts follow the job.
stretch: "Fungi have cell walls but no chloroplasts. What does that suggest
  about how they get food? (They don't photosynthesise: they absorb food from
  what they grow on.)"
support: "Give a two-column table to fill: Part | Plant only or both | Job."
leads: >
  Next: Why are cells different shapes? (specialisation, AC9S8U02 node 1).


  In class: onion skin and Elodea leaf (chloroplasts visible) beside cheek
  cells; wilted and crisp lettuce in salt water and fresh water.
exit:
  q: Name two parts a leaf cell has that a cheek cell lacks, and say what each
    does.
  a: "Any two of: cell wall (support), chloroplasts (photosynthesis), large
    vacuole (keeps the cell firm, stores sap)."
explain: >
  Plant cells have three parts animal cells don't: a **cell wall** for support,
  **chloroplasts** for photosynthesis and a **large vacuole** that keeps the
  cell firm.


  Both have **mitochondria** (release energy) and **ribosomes** (make proteins).
  How many of each a cell has depends on its job.
```
